title: 1MW No. 317: Why People Don't Tell You What They Mean
author: McKeown, Greg
summary: Greg McKeown uses interrogator Eric Maddox's experience hunting for Saddam Hussein to illustrate a listening failure common among problem-solvers: reaching for a solution the moment someone says something incomplete, rather than staying curious long enough for the real signal to emerge. Maddox's scripted interrogation approach failed until a prisoner told him bluntly that he wasn't being understood; shifting from extracting information to understanding the prisoner's actual concerns produced the 'breadcrumbs' that eventually led to Saddam's capture. McKeown applies this directly to everyday conversations: when someone says 'I'm fine' or 'it's not a big deal,' the first statement is rarely the heart of the matter, and jumping to solve it shortcuts the process of making it safe for the real signal to surface.
points: Make it safe for the signal to emerge — don't rush to solve the first thing someone says, since it's rarely the heart of the matter.
Interrogator Eric Maddox's breakthrough came from switching to understanding what a prisoner wanted him to know, rather than steering toward what he wanted to extract.
'Breadcrumbs' — small, seemingly minor disclosures — accumulate into the real picture only if you keep following them instead of pushing harder.
Problem-solvers habitually take people's first words at face value ('I'm fine,' 'it's not a big deal') and move on, missing what's underneath.
Practical move: when something feels incomplete, resist solving it — ask 'What do you mean by that?' or 'Tell me more,' then stay curious.
quotes: Maddox had been listening for information he could use. He wasn’t trying to understand the world from the prisoner’s point of view.
the first thing someone says isn't usually the heart of the matter.
We don’t always have to solve what we hear. We just need to stay curious long enough and make it safe enough for the signal to emerge.
This week, when someone says something that feels incomplete, resist the urge to solve it.
The prisoner eventually revealed that he wanted to help capture the commander who had drawn his brother into the insurgency, but feared putting his family in danger.
